name: Accounting basics
description: Double entry, debits and credits, accrual accounting, and the vocabulary every Zenskar conversation uses.
takeaways: Every entry has equal debits and credits
Revenue is not the invoice amount
Deferred = prepaid = liability; unbilled = postpaid = asset

learn.intro: You will be selling to controllers, revenue accountants and CFOs. This module is the minimum vocabulary to run a credible call. Zenskar's accounting is based on ASC 606.

cards.title: Double-entry
cards.body: Every transaction is entered twice: one debit and one credit, equal and opposite. Nothing is recorded once. If the sides disagree, something is wrong and you can find it.
cards.example: Sell a product for $200 cash: Dr Cash $200, Cr Sales revenue $200.

cards.title: Debits and credits are directions
cards.body: Neither is good or bad. Which direction increases an account depends on the type of account. Total debits must equal total credits in every entry.
cards.example: A debit raises an asset such as cash, but lowers a liability such as deferred revenue.

cards.title: The accounting equation
cards.body: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Assets are what the company owns, liabilities are what it owes others, equity is what is left for the owners.
cards.example: Two founders put $50 each into a shop: $100 cash (asset) against $100 equity.

cards.title: Cheat sheet
cards.body: Debit increases assets and expenses. Credit increases liabilities, equity and revenue. The opposite side decreases them.
cards.example: Customer pays $100: Dr Cash $100 (asset up), Cr Accounts Receivable $100 (asset down).

cards.title: Accrual vs cash accounting
cards.body: Accrual records revenue and expenses when they are earned or incurred. Cash accounting records them when money moves.
cards.example: A $12,000 annual invoice raised in January: cash basis books $12,000 in January; accrual books it as service is delivered.

cards.title: Matching principle
cards.body: Income earned sits in the same period as the expenses incurred to earn it.
cards.example: Service delivered in December and paid in January is December revenue, and December expense.

cards.title: Revenue is not the invoice amount
cards.body: Invoicing is a commercial choice (prepaid or postpaid, monthly or annual). Revenue is recognised as service is delivered. Over a contract the two totals agree; month to month they rarely do.
cards.example: $12,000 billed annually upfront recognises $1,000 a month.

cards.title: ASC 606, IFRS 15, Ind AS 115
cards.body: One framework with three names, five steps: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, recognise revenue.
cards.example: If a client asks which one Zenskar supports, the answer is the framework, not the jurisdiction.

subs.title: The balances you will discuss daily

cards.title: Deferred revenue
cards.body: Invoiced or paid for service not yet delivered. A liability: you owe the customer that service. It burns down as you deliver.
cards.example: An annual prepaid invoice of $1,200 starts with $1,200 deferred and drops $100 a month.

cards.title: Unbilled revenue
cards.body: Service delivered but not yet invoiced. An asset (accrued revenue). It converts to accounts receivable when you invoice. Common with usage and postpaid billing.
cards.example: January usage with the invoice raised on Feb 1: January's revenue is unbilled until then.

cards.title: Accounts receivable
cards.body: Money customers owe you for service already delivered, backed by an invoice. A current asset. It rises at invoice approval and clears when the customer pays.
cards.example: Approve a $1,200 invoice: AR up $1,200. Customer pays: AR down, cash up.

cards.title: AR is not revenue
cards.body: AR is an invoicing event. Only deferred and unbilled balances convert into revenue.
cards.example: An invoice for last month's usage raises AR, but that revenue was already counted as unbilled.

cards.title: Invoiced vs earned
cards.body: Invoiced more than earned means deferred revenue. Earned more than invoiced means unbilled revenue.
cards.example: A client who bills annually upfront carries a large deferred balance; one who bills in arrears on usage carries unbilled.

cards.title: The three statements
cards.body: The P&L covers a period. The balance sheet is a snapshot on one date. The cash flow statement shows where cash came from and went.
cards.example: Cash timing and revenue timing rarely match.

cards.title: Period close
cards.body: Books close monthly. Once a period is locked it cannot change; corrections land in a later month.
cards.example: Books closed in September; an error found in October is corrected in October's books.

cards.title: Materiality
cards.body: An auditor decides whether a difference is large enough to matter. You surface the gap; the client's auditor or CFO decides the treatment.
cards.example: Subscription differences usually pass; usage overages often do not.

cards.title: Where Zenskar sits
cards.body: The ERP holds the general ledger. Zenskar manages the subset related to revenue and creates entries that sync to the ERP.
cards.example: Zenskar has data for revenue, deferred, unbilled, AR, customer cash, gateway fees and sales tax. It does not have payroll, loans or inventory.

learn.outro: Source note: built from the internal Accounting Fundamentals deck and an internal training call, plus Zenskar's public docs.

edgeCases: Labels backwards. Deferred revenue is a liability; unbilled revenue is an asset. Getting them reversed in front of a CFO is costly.
Revenue equals billing. A common client mistake. It is wrong, and it makes reporting to shareholders and auditors inaccurate.
AR rising, revenue flat. Usually customers paying late, not growth. High AR with strong sales means cash is tied up.
Cash-basis clients. Some small clients still run cash accounting. Moving them to accrual leads to a prior-period adjustment conversation.
Monthly vs daily recognition. Both give the same annual total; monthly figures differ for 28, 30 and 31 day months. The client's accountant decides.
Equity. Profits are transferred into equity, so revenue increases equity and expense decreases it.
Scope. Zenskar does not hold payroll, loan, operating expense or inventory data. Imported opening balances cover what existed before go-live.

quiz.question: Why is deferred revenue a liability?
options: You were paid for service you still owe the customer
It is cash held for suppliers
quiz.explanation: You hold the customer's money against a promise to deliver service, so it sits on the liability side until earned.

quiz.question: A customer pays an outstanding invoice of $100. Which entry is right?
quiz.explanation: Cash (asset) goes up with a debit and receivables (asset) go down with a credit. Revenue is not touched at payment.

quiz.question: A client bills $60,000 annually upfront on 1 April and recognises straight-line by month. What is the deferred balance on 30 June?
quiz.explanation: Three months are earned ($15,000), so $45,000 remains deferred.

quiz.question: You earned more than you have invoiced. What do you hold?
quiz.explanation: Service delivered but not invoiced is unbilled revenue, an asset that becomes AR at invoicing.

quiz.question: Which is the correct order of the five ASC 606 steps?
quiz.explanation: Identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the price, allocate it, then recognise revenue.

qa.question: Debit vs credit?
qa.answer: They are the two sides of an entry. Neither is good or bad. A debit raises assets and expenses and lowers liabilities, equity and revenue; a credit does the reverse.

qa.question: Deferred revenue vs unbilled revenue?
qa.answer: Deferred revenue is paid or invoiced but not yet delivered, a liability. Unbilled revenue is delivered but not yet invoiced, an asset. Compare what you invoiced to what you earned.

qa.question: Accounts receivable vs revenue?
qa.answer: AR is an invoicing event: money you are owed. Revenue is earned through delivery. AR can rise with no new revenue if customers pay late.

qa.question: Accrual vs cash accounting?
qa.answer: Accrual records when earned or incurred, cash records when money moves. On a $12,000 annual invoice, cash accounting books all of it at once while accrual spreads it across the service period.

qa.question: Bookings vs billings vs revenue vs cash?
qa.answer: Bookings are contracted value signed, billings are amounts invoiced, revenue is what has been earned under the accounting rules, cash is money received. They rarely match in a given month.

qa.question: Balance sheet vs P&L vs cash flow statement?
qa.answer: The balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity on one date. The P&L covers a period of revenue and expense. The cash flow statement tracks cash movement.

qa.question: ASC 606 vs IFRS 15 vs Ind AS 115?
qa.answer: They are the US, international and Indian names for the same five-step revenue framework. For our purposes they are functionally equivalent.

qa.question: Liability vs equity?
qa.answer: Liabilities are owed to others (loans, payables, deferred revenue, sales tax). Equity is what is left for the owners after liabilities are covered.

qa.question: A client bills annually upfront. What will their balance sheet show?
qa.answer: A large deferred revenue balance (a liability) that steps down as service is delivered.

qa.question: A client bills monthly in arrears on usage. What will dominate?
qa.answer: Unbilled revenue (an asset) that grows through the month and clears when the invoice is raised.

qa.question: A customer asks why revenue is not equal to their invoices.
qa.answer: Invoicing is a commercial decision; revenue follows delivery. Over the contract life the totals match, but month to month they differ, and managing that gap is what Zenskar does.

qa.question: A client has no service logs and sets revenue equal to billing. What do you do?
qa.answer: Surface the gap and its risk (compliance, reporting, audit). The client's auditor or CFO decides the treatment. You compute and show; you do not decide.

qa.question: A customer prepays $10,000, draws it down, then pays overage. Where does the money go?
qa.answer: The prepayment starts as deferred revenue and is recognised as it is consumed. Usage beyond the prepaid amount is unbilled until it is invoiced.

qa.question: Can an entry have debits that differ from credits?
qa.answer: No. In double-entry accounting total debits equal total credits in every entry. If they differ, something is wrong.

qa.question: AR is climbing while revenue is flat. What is happening?
qa.answer: Likely customers are paying late. The CFO cares because cash is tied up and near-term obligations may be hard to meet.

qa.question: The books are closed and you find an error.
qa.answer: You cannot reopen the period. The correction lands in a later month, and an auditor judges whether the difference is material.

qa.question: Is deferred revenue free money?
qa.answer: The cash is in the bank and no interest is paid on it, but it is still a liability because you owe the service. Leverage sits with the customer.

qa.question: Does recognising by day vs by month change the annual total?
qa.answer: No. Both sum to the same annual figure; monthly numbers differ for 28, 30 and 31 day months.

qa.question: Does Zenskar hold payroll or loan data?
qa.answer: No. It holds the revenue-related subset of the general ledger: revenue, deferred, unbilled, AR, customer cash, gateway fees and sales tax.

qa.question: What happens in the books when an invoice is approved?
qa.answer: Accounts receivable goes up. For a future-period prepaid invoice the other side is deferred revenue; for service already delivered it clears unbilled revenue.

qa.question: Why does Zenskar sit on top of an ERP?
qa.answer: The ERP is the single source of truth, but billing is its weakest area. Zenskar handles complex pricing and revenue entries and syncs them to the ERP.

qa.question: What is the matching principle?
qa.answer: Income earned belongs in the same period as the expenses incurred to earn it, regardless of when cash moves.
